standard.title: Locate and identify sources
standard.description: locate and identify primary and secondary sources to use in historical inquiry
standard.prior_knowledge: Students locate and identify primary and secondary sources to use in historical inquiry (AC9HH7S02). They can identify and categorise sources. They have not yet organised sources into systematic categories (written, visual, material culture, artefacts), retrieved information from multiple digital repositories using advanced search functions, or evaluated the range and diversity of their source base.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students locate and identify primary and secondary sources to use in historical inquiry — organising them by type and period, retrieving information from digital repositories using advanced search techniques, and assembling a diverse source base appropriate to the inquiry.

nodes.label: Categorising sources
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can categorise sources by type — primary vs secondary, and written, visual, material culture and artefacts — and explain what each category can and cannot tell us about the past.
nodes.minimum_width: Correct categorisation of at least four sources using the primary/secondary and type categories.
nodes.typical_width: Systematic categorisation across all source types with explanation of what each type offers as evidence. Primary sources from the period: journals, church records, paintings, artefacts, sites. Secondary sources: fictional interpretations, artistic interpretations, academic texts. Understanding that some sources are ambiguous (e.g. a contemporary novel about a medieval event).
wider: Examine a specific source (e.g. Boccaccio's Decameron, Viking sagas, Zhou Daguan's account of the Khmer) and determine its category — considering that literary sources can be both primary (evidence of attitudes) and secondary (interpretation of events)

Investigate how the category of a source affects how it can be used in a historical inquiry — e.g. a painting of the Black Death as evidence of contemporary attitudes vs a modern photograph of Angkor Wat as evidence of the site's current state
nodes.hinge_reason: Miscategorising sources leads to misuse in inquiry — treating secondary sources as direct evidence of events, or treating all primary sources as equally reliable. Correct categorisation is prerequisite to source analysis in S03 and S04.

response_modes.reason: Source categorisation requires repeated practice with varied examples before it becomes reliable. Students need multiple opportunities to categorise sources of different types and periods before the distinctions become automatic.

success_criteria: Correctly categorises at least four sources as primary or secondary and by type (written, visual, material culture, artefact)
Explains what each source type can and cannot tell us about the past

nodes.label: Locating sources digitally
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can retrieve relevant information from multiple digital sources — including repositories of primary sources, maps and photographs of artefacts — using advanced search functions to refine results.
nodes.minimum_width: Use of at least two different digital source types with at least one example of using advanced search functions (e.g. filters, date ranges, search terms) to refine results.
nodes.typical_width: Systematic use of digital repositories to locate primary sources; use of online platforms hosting maps, photographs of culturally significant artefacts, and academic databases; understanding of how to assess the relevance of retrieved sources before committing to using them.
wider: Compare two searches on the same topic using different search strategies (broad vs specific terms, with vs without filters) to examine how search design affects the quality of retrieved sources

Investigate how to locate primary sources from non-European medieval societies (e.g. Islamic manuscripts, Chinese diplomatic records, Icelandic sagas) using digital repositories, examining how the availability of digitised sources varies by culture and period

response_modes.reason: Digital source retrieval is a procedural skill that requires practice with real repositories. Students need hands-on experience with multiple searches before they can reliably locate relevant sources and assess their relevance.

success_criteria: Retrieves relevant sources from at least two different digital repositories or source types
Uses at least one advanced search technique (filters, date ranges, specific search terms) and explains how it improved the search results
